coredata.dc:description:
Background The healthcare industry faces a major concern; a high rate of turnover intention (TOI), which poses significant risks to patient well-being, stability of healthcare systems, and performance of healthcare organizations. Nonetheless, there is limited literature on this topic in sub-Saharan Africa, a region deemed at-risk. This study, therefore, examined the predictors of TOI among health workers in the Greater Accra Region of Ghana.
Methods This study used an analytic cross-sectional design and was conducted in selected health facilities in the Greater Accra region between January 30 and May 31, 2023. Participants were selected through proportionate-to-size simple random sampling. Data analysis was conducted using Stata version 15, and factors linked to TOI were determined through log-binomial regression at a statistical significance of p < 0.05.
Results The study, which involved 495 health workers across 10 private and district hospitals, found a TOI prevalence of 59.8% [95% CI: 55.3%–64.1%]. Supporting staff category [APR = 1.59 (1.10, 2.32)], worked over 5 days weekly, [APR = 1.19 (1.01, 1.39)], overtime work [APR = 1.26 (1.08, 1.46)], perceived understaff [APR = 1.40 (1.18, 1.67)], exposure to physical assault [APR = 1.21 (1.05, 1.40)], and 8 h or more of daily sleep [(APR = 0.77 (0.64, 0.94)] were factors significantly associated with TOI.
Conclusion The prevalence of TOI was lower compared to other regional studies. Supporting staff category, number of working days per week, overtime work, daily hours of sleep, perceived understaff, and exposure to physical assault were factors influencing TOI among health workers in Ghana. Health stakeholders should consider ways of addressing these issues to reduce health worker’s intention to quit their job.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The healthcare industry faces a major concern; a high rate of turnover intention (TOI), which poses significant risks to patient well-being, stability of healthcare systems, and performance of healthcare organizations. Nonetheless, there is limited literature on this topic in sub-Saharan Africa, a region deemed at-risk. This study, therefore, examined the predictors of TOI among health workers in the Greater Accra Region of Ghana.

This study used an analytic cross-sectional design and was conducted in selected health facilities in the Greater Accra region between January 30 and May 31, 2023. Data analysis was conducted using Stata version 15, and factors linked to TOI were determined through log-binomial regression at a statistical significance of p < 0.05.

Supporting staff category, number of working days per week, overtime work, daily hours of sleep, perceived understaff, and exposure to physical assault were factors influencing TOI among health workers in Ghana. Health stakeholders should consider ways of addressing these issues to reduce health worker’s intention to quit their job.

ce:data-availability.ce:para: The datasets analysed during the current study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

ce:section.ce:para: The healthcare industry is confronting a critical challenge: a substantial proportion of health workers are considering exit from their positions, posing significant threats to patient safety, healthcare system resilience, and organizational performance [1,2]. Unless addressed, this trend may have far-reaching consequences, including a drop in the quality of care provided, an increase in avoidable errors, and a decrease in patient satisfaction, which could ultimately erode confidence in the healthcare system [3]. On a global scale, there was an approximate shortage of 7.2 million health workers [4]. The scarcity of workers is particularly pronounced in Africa, especially in sub-Saharan countries, where the health worker-to-population ratio is the lowest [5]. In Ghana, the density of health worker per 1000 population is calculated to be 2.32 [6], which is lower than the global average of 9.3 [5].

Worldwide, the healthcare workforce is grappling with unprecedented levels of exhaustion, anxiety, and discontent which can lead to turnover intention (TOI), an employee’s conscious and deliberate willingness to leave their current organization within a certain timeframe [7]. Turnover intention serves as a significant predictor of actual employee turnover and is often assessed to understand and mitigate factors leading to staff attrition [8]. In recent times, TOI has become a widespread concern among health workers including doctors, nurses, midwives, laboratory staff, physiotherapist, and even supporting staff, with studies indicating that more than half of them contemplate leaving their current positions [9,10]. However, majority of earlier studies concentrated on nurses and midwives. Therefore, it is imperative to consider the holistic view of TOI among health workers across various occupational groups. Also, numerous literature has shown that TOI is influenced by a range of demographic and personal characteristics [11], especially gender and profession. Organizational and occupational related factors such as job satisfaction [12], nature of work [13], work environment [13], autonomy [14], supervision [15], renumerations [16] and peer group relationships [17] have been explored and linked to TOI. Research examining the link between TOI and exposure to occupational health hazards such as needlestick injuries, body fluid splashes, verbal abuse, sexual harassment, and physical assault in healthcare settings remains scarce.

A plethora of studies have been conducted on the TOI of health workers across the globe. For example, a Chinese systematic review and meta-analysis reported that general practitioners worldwide had an average turnover intention prevalence of 47% [18]. Additionally, a similar review conducted among health workers in Ethiopia found a pooled nationwide TOI prevalence of 58.1% [19]. Furthermore, additional research on TOI among health workers in Ethiopia and Ghana indicated prevalence rates of 61.3% (20) and 69.0% [20], respectively. Though the forementioned high estimates of TOI project the intensity of actual attrition among health professionals in different parts of the world, factors contributing to TOI among health workers in specific regions and areas like Ghana, a West African country, remains not fully understood.

This paper contributes to the existing body of knowledge by broadening the focus of TOI research beyond nurses and midwives to include a wider spectrum of health workers such as doctors, laboratory staff, physiotherapists, and supporting staff. By doing so, it addresses a critical gap in the literature, offering a more holistic understanding of TOI across occupational groups. Furthermore, while previous studies have largely centred on demographic, organizational, and job-related factors, this study enhances our understanding by examining the underexplored relationship between TOI and exposure to occupational health hazards - including needlestick injuries, exposure to body fluids, verbal abuse, sexual harassment, and physical assault. These hazards are particularly relevant in the current healthcare environment but have received limited scholarly attention. Exposure to these hazards increases stress and job dissatisfaction. Also, these hazards undermine workers’ sense of safety and well-being, prompting them to consider leaving their roles.

The study therefore examined the predicting factors of turnover intention among health workers in Greater Accra, the capital region of Ghana. Additionally, the study examined the relationship between exposure to specific occupational hazards, such as needlestick injuries, verbal abuse, sexual harassment and physical assault, and their association with TOI of health workers. By investigating these factors, this study sought to shed light on the underlying causes of TOI and inform strategies to mitigate this critical issue in the healthcare workforce.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Research design, study population, and setting
ce:section.ce:para: This research employed an analytic, facility-based cross-sectional design using a quantitative methodology. It focused on a range of health and support personnel including doctors, nurses, midwives, laboratory and physiotherapy staff, healthcare assistants, orderlies, and laundry personnel across ten major hospitals in Ghana’s Greater Accra region. Of these hospitals, six were publicly managed while the remaining four were private. The hospitals selected for this study included Weija-Gbawe Municipal Hospital, Ashaiman Community Hospital, Pentecost Hospital, Sakumono Community Hospital, Nyaho Medical Centre, Shai-Osudoku Hospital, Tema General Hospital, Achimota Hospital, LEKMA Hospital, and Ga North Municipal Hospital. These hospitals serve as primary healthcare hubs in their respective districts, providing a comprehensive range of medical services, including outpatient care, maternal and child health, dental care, ophthalmology, laboratory tests, ENT services, radiology, and dermatology. Additionally, they also offer surgical interventions. The bed capacity of these facilities varies from 50 to 500. The total number of health workers and supporting staff in all the 10 facilities was 3054. In 2015, the Greater Accra region accounted for approximately 30.6% of Ghana’s total health workforce, including medical officers, midwives, nurses, and pharmacists, making it the region with the highest concentration of health professionals in the country [21]. Furthermore, data from 2022 reveals that 42.0% of Ghana’s medical doctors were based in Accra, underscoring the capital city’s dominance in healthcare personnel [22]. In 2021, the Greater Accra Region was Ghana’s most densely populated region, with an estimated 5,455,692 residents, representing roughly 17.7% of the national population [23].

The sample size for this study was calculated using the Cochran formula,

Assuming a 95% confidence level (z = 1.96), a proportion (p) of 67.8% based on a recent study conducted among health workers in Ethiopia [25], a margin of error (d) of 5%, and q as (1 – p), the initial sample size was estimated at 335. To account for clustering, a design effect of 1.5 was applied, as recommended in previous studies [26]. Also, considering a 10% non-response rate, the final sample size was adjusted to 553.

A multi-stage sampling strategy was adopted for this study. The Greater Accra region of Ghana was purposively chosen as the study area. Subsequently, districts, hospitals, and individual participants were randomly selected. This process was guided by a probability proportional-to-size method to ensure representativeness. The region comprises 29 districts - 2 metropolitan, 23 municipal, and 4 district assemblies. From these, 10 districts (representing over 30% of the total) were included in the study. The sampling frame consisted of 17 major hospitals, out of which 10 were randomly chosen. Generally, one major hospital was selected per district. In cases where a district had multiple major hospitals, one hospital was randomly selected. The choice of hospitals was informed by outpatient department (OPD) attendance records from the 2021 District Health Information Management System (DHIMS) [27]. Hospitals with the highest outpatient department (OPD) attendance, as recorded in the District Health Information Management System (DHIMS), were designated as the major facilities in the study’s sampling frame. Participants for this study were selected using stratified random sampling, ensuring a representative mix of study participants from each occupational group. A computer-generated randomization process was employed to randomly select individuals from each occupational group. The study participants included doctors, nurses, midwives, laboratory personnel, physiotherapists, and support staff. Health professionals who had worked in a hospital for at least one year were eligible to take part. However, health students on internship at selected hospitals were not included.

Data were gathered using a structured questionnaire. Although the instrument was developed for this study, parts of it were adapted from a previously validated “Healthcare Workers Safety and Health Survey” originating from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and other published studies [28,29]. The questionnaire primarily consisted of closed-ended items and was divided into three sections: Section I addressed participants’ socio-demographic details and lifestyle characteristics (11 items); Section II focused on occupational variables (9 items); and Section III explored TOI (6 items). The questions on the dependent variable, TOI were ranked on a 5-Likert scale [28]. Turnover intention was defined as the likelihood of leaving one’s current position, with respondents indicating a desire to depart from their role at some point in the future.

A pilot test was conducted with 30 health workers at Ho Teaching Hospital to assess the questionnaire’s clarity and relevance. Based on the feedback received from participants, academic experts in occupational health and safety, and senior officials of the Ghana Health Service, necessary revisions were made to improve the instrument. Data were collected using paper-based questionnaires. After a short introduction, participants were given the self-administered questionnaire along with instructions to complete it without delay. Participants were allowed to return their completed questionnaires by the following day. When participants encountered difficulties in completing the forms, research assistants stepped in to conduct interviews using the questionnaire. Responses from paper-based questionnaires were entered into the Open Data Kit (ODK) electronic platform. The participant recruitment and data collection occurred between January 30 and May 31, 2023.

Data were exported from the Open Data Kit platform into STATA SE version 15 (64 bit) for both cleaning and subsequent analysis. An initial quality check was performed to detect and correct any errors. Quantitative variables were evaluated using skewness and kurtosis tests to determine suitability for parametric versus nonparametric analyses. Descriptive statistics included frequencies and percentages for categorical data, while continuous variables were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges. Socio-demographic, lifestyle, and occupational factors, which served as the independent variables, were presented in tabular format. In contrast, TOI, the dependent variable, was displayed graphically using a pie chart. The assessment of TOI involved 6 questions ranked on a 5-Likert scale [28]. A score from 16 to 30 was categorized as ‘Yes’ for TOI, while a score ranging from 0 to 15 was categorized as ‘No’ for TOI.

Preliminary analysis examined the association between TOI and each independent variable using chi-square, Fisher’s exact, and Mann–Whitney U tests. Variables with a p-value of 0.1 or less in these tests were subsequently included in the bivariate log-binomial regression analysis. Additionally, multiple log-binomial regression analyses were conducted to confirm the association between the independent variables and the prevalence of TOI, using a significance level of p < 0.05. To evaluate potential multicollinearity among the primary explanatory variables, Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) were calculated. Variables with VIF values greater than 5, including marital status, highest educational level, type of health facility, and workplace pressure, were removed. After these adjustments, the remaining variables showed no indication of multicollinearity, with mean VIF of 2.11, minimum VIF of 1.27, and maximum VIF of 3.23.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Socio-demographic and lifestyle characteristics of health workers
ce:section.ce:para: Table 1 provides an overview of healthcare workers selected from ten major hospitals in Ghana’s Greater Accra Region. Out of the estimated sample size (553), 495 health workers that participated in the study, reflecting a response rate of 89.5%. Over half of the participants, 269 (54.3%), were nurses, while slightly more than one in ten, 56 (11.3%), served as supporting staff. Most of the participants, 312 (53.1%) were within the 30 – 39-year-old bracket; and the median age was 32 years, with an interquartile range of 28 - 37 years. The dominant group of the participants, 410 (82.8%) were females, and almost half (48.1%) were married. Most of the study respondents, 451 (91.1%) had attained tertiary education. Also, many study respondents, 146 (29.5%) were earning within 1000 – 1900 Ghana cedis ($64.5 – $129.0); with the median income of 2000 Ghana cedis ($129.1), and an interquartile range of 1000 to 3500 Ghana cedis ($64.5 – $225.9). In addition, 437 participants (88.3%) were employed in government-owned health facilities, and 430 (86.9%) held permanent positions. The majority, 385 (77.8%), reported working five days or fewer per week, while 371 (75.0%) slept less than 8 h each day.

As shown in Table 2 , most of the respondents, 272 (55.0%), reported working overtime. Nearly half, 245 (49.5%), indicated that they occasionally felt work-related pressure. Additionally, 270 participants (54.6%) experienced moderate levels of stress, while 336 (67.9%) representing more than two thirds perceived their departments as being understaffed. Regarding occupational exposures, majority of participants, 300 (60.6%) had experienced needlestick injuries, and more than three-quarters, 404 (81.6%) had been exposed to splash of body fluids. Also, over two-thirds, 335 (67.7%) had been verbally abused by clients or colleagues, and one-tenth, 51 (10.3%) had been harassed sexually at their health facilities. Furthermore, a little over one-quarter, 142 (28.7%) had been physically assaulted at the workplace.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Prevalence of turnover intention among health workers
ce:section.ce:para: Overall, a greater portion of health workers, 296 (59.8%) [95% CI: (55.3%-64.1%)] showed TOI (Fig. 1 ).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Socio-demographic and lifestyle characteristics influencing turnover intention
ce:section.ce:para: A statistically significant relationship was observed between marital status ( χ2 = 7.86, p = 0.020), educational level ( χ2 = 9.74, p = 0.002), and TOI. Also, type of health facility ( χ2 = 6.12, p = 0.013), daily hours of sleep ( χ2 = 8.96, p = 0.003), and number of working days in a typical week ( χ2 = 4.14, p = 0.042) were related to TOI (Table 3 ).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Occupational related factors influencing turnover intention
ce:section.ce:para: As shown in Table 4 , a significant association was revealed between overtime ( χ2 = 14.06, p < 0.001), pressure from work ( χ2 = 21.10, p < 0.001), understaff ( χ2 = 17.12, p < 0.001), and TOI. Additionally, exposure to physical assault ( χ2 = 8.96, p = 0.003) was associated with TOI.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Factors associated with turnover intention among health workers
ce:section.ce:para: Table 5 below summarizes the bivariate and multiple log-binomial regression analysis between TOI and its predictors. Apart from verbal abuse, all variables on the bivariate log-binomial regression model were significant. The multivariate log-binomial regression analysis showed that TOI was significantly associated with occupation, average daily sleep duration, number of working days per week, overtime work, perceived understaffing, and experience of physical assault. Supporting staff showed a higher prevalence of TOI (adjusted prevalence ratio - APR = 1.59, 95% CI = 1.10 – 2.32, p = 0.015) than those in the doctors’ profession. Additionally, working more than five days a week was associated with a higher prevalence of TOI (APR = 1.19, 95% CI = 1.01-1.39, p = 0.033), compared to working five days or less. Working overtime (APR = 1.26, 95% CI = 1.08-1.46, p = 0.003) was also associated with a higher prevalence of TOI, compared to not working overtime. Perceiving understaffing in their department (APR = 1.40, 95% CI = 1.18-1.67, p < 0.001) was associated with a higher prevalence of TOI among health workers, compared to those who did not perceive staffing shortages. Health workers who had experienced physical assault was associated with a higher prevalence of turnover intention (APR = 1.21, 95% CI: 1.05 to 1.40, p = 0.008) compared to those who had not. In contrast, individuals who reported sleeping at least 8 h per day had a lower likelihood of turnover intention (APR = 0.77, 95% CI: 0.64 to 0.94, p = 0.009) than those who slept for fewer hours.

This research explored the predictors of TOI among Ghanaian health workers, including the influence of occupational health hazards on their likelihood of intending to leave their jobs. More than half, 296 (59.8%) of health workers expressed TOI. Supporting staff had a higher prevalence of TOI. Health workers who worked more than five days a week, engaged in overtime, perceived understaffing in their departments, or experienced physical assault showed a higher prevalence of turnover intention. However, prevalence of TOI was lower among health workers who had daily sleep of 8 h and above.

According to our study, a substantial number of health workers in the Ghanaian industry showed TOI. This outcome was comparable to a systematic review and meta-analysis conducted among health workers in Ethiopia (58.1%) [30]. However, our result was higher than the pooled prevalence of TOI (47.0%) [18] among general practitioners in the world. Moreover, the prevalence of turnover intention (TOI) reported in cross-sectional studies from Ethiopia (61.3%) [31] and Ghana (69.0%) [20] was higher than the proportion observed in the present study. The variability in these percentages is likely to be influenced by several factors including diverse nature of job roles and responsibilities, coupled with variations in work environments and settings, opportunities for professional growth and development, workload intensity, autonomy in decision-making, and the level of support received from colleagues and supervisors. However, in Ghana, the prominent factors are the degree of job satisfaction and engagement, as well as disparities in compensation and benefits packages [20,32,33].

Supporting staff had a higher prevalence of TOI. Though there is lack of literature that examines TOI among supporting staff, or reports higher prevalence among them, a similar study [34] implied that supporting staff, including housekeeping and other non-clinical staff, had a higher likelihood of intending to leave their jobs compared to clinical staff, such as nurses and doctors because they have lower perceptions of control, job satisfaction, and managerial support, which may contribute to their TOI. In the Ghanaian setting, supporting staff may encounter distinct difficulties and pressures that drive their intention to quit, including inadequate acknowledgment of their efforts, excessive workload and extended working hours, restricted access to career growth and advancement opportunities, suboptimal work environments and resource scarcity, and limited independence and decision-making capacity [35,36].

Further, the study found that health workers who worked for more than 5 days in week, and did overtime work showed higher prevalence of TOI. Our finding was consistent with studies conducted in many parts of the world including Ethiopia [37], Taiwan [38], and South Korea [39]. Working overtime increases the risk of burnout, which in turn leads to higher TOI [40]. Besides, overtime work is associated with increased stress levels, which can lead to adverse health outcomes and unhealthy behaviours such as lack of physical activity. Both factors can negatively impact health workers’ well-being, leading to decreased job satisfaction and commitment, which in turn may increase TOI rates [41]. These instances echo the significance of overtime in people expressing intention of leaving their jobs.

Another outcome of the study revealed that health professionals who perceived understaffing in their department showed higher prevalence of TOI. A recent study confirmed this finding of our research [42]. It is not surprising this result is similar in other countries, especially Africa. Some authors [43,44] mentioned that, being understaffed coupled with factors such as poor job resources, low staff morale, high job demands, and increased workload increases TOI among health workers. Perceived understaffing among health workers has also been linked to TOI, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic [43]. Tackling issues like job-related stress, emotional fatigue, and excessive workload is essential for retaining the limited health workforce and maintaining stability within the healthcare system.

Further, our study showed that health professionals who experienced physical assault showed higher prevalence of TOI. Physical assault as a risk factor for TOI was also confirmed in a study conducted among health professionals in Turkey [45]. Though physical assault as a form of workplace violence has not been well explored in literature, few studies like ours highlights their contribution to TOI. However, numerous studies [46,47] have related general workplace violence to health workers expressing intention of leaving their jobs. According to a recent study, the authors opined that workplace violence against health care workers was exacerbated by COVID-19 and can be influenced by future pandemics, and this occupational risk should be considered when evaluating nurses and health professional exposure to violence, as it affects job satisfaction and TOI [48].

Furthermore, this study found that prevalence of TOI was lower among health workers who had daily sleep of 8 h and above. This outcome was similar to a study where patient care workers with more schedule controlled reported greater sleep duration and quality leading to lower TOI [49]. Although there was lack of studies that researched directly into the association between the ability to sleep for 8 h and above, and TOI among health workers, related studies reveals that sleep disturbance and poor sleep were related to higher odds of TOI [30,50]. Also, a study highlighted sleep disorders or sleep duration as some of the factors that could be addressed to reduce TOI among health workers, particularly nurses [51].

Finally, our study findings have significant implications for healthcare practice, policy, and future research, particularly within the context of Ghana’s healthcare system. Healthcare organizations must prioritize comprehensive and context-specific strategies to mitigate turnover intention (TOI) among healthcare supporting staff, who play a vital role in maintaining the functionality of the healthcare system. Policies should address excessive workload, long hours, and inadequate staffing by ensuring equitable staff-to-patient ratios and enforcing manageable shift schedules to minimize burnout. Improving compensation packages, providing clear career progression pathways, and recognizing outstanding performance through awards or incentives can further enhance retention.

Additionally, creating a safe and supportive work environment is essential. This includes enforcing strict policies against physical and verbal abuse, installing security measures in high-risk departments, and offering training in conflict resolution. Promoting healthy sleep habits and stress management should go beyond awareness campaigns to include access to mental health services, employee wellness programs, and regular counselling sessions. Future research should evaluate the effectiveness of these interventions and investigate additional factors influencing TOI, such as rural-urban posting disparities, transportation challenges, and the availability of housing near health facilities. By proactively addressing these issues, Ghana’s healthcare system can improve job satisfaction, retain skilled personnel, and ultimately enhance the overall quality of patient care.

The study’s strength lies in its real-world applicability and large-scale data collection across private and district hospitals in Ghana’s National Capital. This diverse selection enhances the generalizability of findings, making them relevant for policymakers and hospital administrators. Nonetheless, there are specific limitations inherent in this research. The inability to achieve a full response rate was largely attributed to the absence of financial motivation for participants. The cross-sectional design limits the ability to establish clear cause-and-effect relationships or determine the sequence of influencing factors. Additionally, relying on participants’’ memory of events over the past year introduces the risk of recall bias. Finally, the findings of this study should be interpreted alongside related published work conducted among the same study population. This prior study by our team examined turnover intention in relation to low back pain among healthcare workers, assessing turnover intention using two items [52]. This partially overlaps with the outcome variable in the present study; however, turnover intention was measured using six items and examined within a different conceptual framework. These differences in outcome measurement and analytical focus provide complementary rather than duplicative evidence. Moreover, the current analysis addresses a distinct research question by exploring turnover intention in relation to some predicting factors including exposure to other occupational hazards such as needlestick injuries, verbal abuse, sexual harassment and physical assault.

The prevalence of TOI among health workers and supporting staff in the Greater Accra region was lower compared to regional studies. Supporting staff category, worked for more than 5 days in a typical week, worked overtime, perceived understaff and exposed to physical assault were significantly associated with a higher prevalence of TOI. Nonetheless, sleeping for 8 h or more was related to lower prevalence of TOI. Health administrators, managers and policy makers should consider ways of addressing the issues of overtime work, physical assault and understaff to reduce the health worker’s TOI. Building on current findings, future investigations can leverage on prospective cohort studies to establish definitive cause-and-effect relationships.
